title: Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily
content_c:
Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars.
A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival.
Dozens of people were reported injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass. Among the most seriously injured was a 70-year-old man admitted to Mazara del Vallo hospital in a critical condition with several fractures.
A school was also hit by the powerful winds, leaving six children with minor cuts and abrasions. At the time the tornado struck, 273 pupils were inside the building, all of whom were safely evacuated. Drone footage showing the aftermath revealed extensive damage to the school, with windows shattered and desks and chairs overturned.
In recent years, people in southern Italy have been bracing for the arrival of a “medicane” – a rare Mediterranean storm with hurricane-like characteristics, capable of producing winds exceeding 60 miles an hour and waves reaching five metres in height.
The weather system developed amid intense heat over north Africa and unusually warm Mediterranean waters. Scientists have warned that rising sea temperatures, driven by the climate emergency, can provide additional energy for powerful storms in the region.
According to experts, record temperatures in the Mediterranean contributed to the freak storm that sank the Bayesian, a super yacht off the coast of Sicily, in August 2024, killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter.
author: Lorenzo Tondo in Palermo

title: ‘Would I sit down with Tommy Robinson? It’s not a definite no’: lessons from people who fought the far right in the 70s, 80s and beyond
content_c:
‘If you’re not organised, you get picked on. When you’re organised, often they flee’
Tariq Mehmood encountered the far right early – at primary school. “When white children surround you in the playground and sing, ‘God made little black people, he made them in the night, he made them in a hurry, and forgot to paint them white’, and the school doesn’t clamp down on that, then you’re living within the far right. It’s not one organisation, it’s a mass movement.”
I think it’s likely those kids used another word for “black people” but I can’t quite find the stomach to ask. Mehmood is speaking to me on a video call from Beirut, where he teaches at the American University. Now 70, he migrated, in 1967, from Pakistan to Bradford, where his grandfather and uncles worked in the textile mills, and immediately experienced racism. “The headmaster would tell us to be grateful to be in England, we were beaten up by white boys on the way to school, there was an intense violence and a feeling of helplessness.”
Until he realised he wasn’t helpless, or alone. “We knew we couldn’t come to school on our own, so we assembled somewhere, got off the bus together and walked together to the classroom.”
Later, when he was himself working in a mill in Otley in the late 70s, Mehmood was one of the founders of the Bradford Asian Youth Movement. The AYMs were a network of anti-racist groups demanding equal rights and a fairer world as well as defending their communities against attacks from groups such as the National Front (NF) and the British Movement (BM).
Following disagreements within the AYM, Mehmood was part of a splinter group, the United Black Youth League, that broke away in 1981. “The police tried to paint that our split was because the UBYL wanted violence, but this is anything but the truth,” he says. “Some wanted to work within the system – one of the founders of the AYM became an MP, something I fundamentally disagreed with then as I do now.”
There were frequent attacks on the south Asian community in Bradford. “Whenever the National Front had a demonstration, you could always bet that after the pubs closed they would attack us, groups of skinheads – five, six, seven of them in a car, going around, seeing what they could do.”
So, as Mehmood had done at school, the UBYL organised themselves. “If you’re not organised, you get picked on. When you’re organised, often they will flee and you don’t have to fight. We couldn’t trust the police; either they were incapable, or they didn’t care, or they harassed us.”
When they learned that a lot of fascists were planning to go to Bradford, they got ready. “We mobilised hundreds, many of them white, walking around, making sure people knew we were out, they didn’t have anything to fear. We said we’d arm ourselves if need be. Some of us made petrol bombs.”
The petrol bombs require some context. “Remember, it was the year of the massacre of the teenagers in London,” he says, referring to the New Cross house fire in which 13 young black people died (even though it was never proved to have been a racist attack). “Members of the UBYL were blocking up their own letter boxes in case someone poured petrol in and set fire to their houses. That was a reality, and we said no, we will defend ourselves.”
In summer 1981, 12 members of the UBYL, including Mehmood, were arrested after a police raid discovered 38 milk bottles filled with petrol. The Bradford 12, as they became known, were charged with conspiracy to cause explosions and endanger lives. They didn’t deny making the molotov cocktails, but said it was a precaution for self-defence.
In jail, awaiting trial, Mehmood discovered another weapon: the pen. He wrote his first novel, Hand on the Sun, about a young immigrant experiencing racism. “Stories make us human. I wanted to share with future generations that we were proud industrial workers, we weren’t just going to have crumbs, we were politically conscious and had hope. I still have that hope.” After an active campaign and a lengthy trial, on 16 June 1982 Mehmood and the rest of the Bradford 12 – who had argued self-defence – were acquitted by a jury.
The situation with the far right is no better today, he says. In fact, the opposite: “The atmosphere is more vicious than it was in the 80s, primarily because we were dealing with old-style racism born out of British colonial history. Today’s Islamophobia is a more violent, virulent form; it has always been there, under the surface, since the Crusades, but not at a scale you see today. The far right at that time were a few thousand demonstrators here and there, not 100,000, half a million. And they’re not just in Britain, but across Europe.”
He sees it as a failure of the left, of the labour and trade union movements, to educate the white working class that “the real enemy is the billionaires at the top”. Plus, the loss of community organisations. Mehmood’s message about what to do about the far right today is to do as they did: organise and fight back. “The most important lesson is that if you believe there is an injustice, then fight against it.”
Tariq Mehmood’s memoir, Rebellion: Self-defence and the Story of the Bradford 12, is published by Daraja Press. A documentary, also titled Rebellion and co-directed by Mehmood, premieres at the BFI London film festival on October 14 and 15
‘The idea was to harness music and politics together to fight fascism and racism’
It was half a century ago, the hot summer of 1976, but Red Saunders remembers it clearly. A photographer and at the time also a member of a radical theatre group, he was in a rehearsal at a studio in Soho, London. “Someone came in and said: ‘Have you seen this shit about Eric Clapton?’”
An article in a music magazine said that at a concert in Birmingham, the musician had told his audience to vote for Enoch “rivers of blood” Powell in order to stop Britain from becoming “a black colony”, as well as chanting the NF slogan: Keep Britain White.
“I was a Clapton fan, I’d been to his gigs, had the albums. I couldn’t believe it,” says Saunders, now 80 and talking to me from his Suffolk home. He wrote a letter to the music press, and got some of his like-minded friends, including Roger Huddle and Jo Wreford to sign it. The letter pointed out Clapton’s hypocrisy, that he was “rock music’s biggest colonialist” and that his own music had its roots in blues, R&B, reggae. And it concluded with a rallying call for musicians and fans to rise up: “Keep the faith, black and white unite and fight.” (Clapton later apologised and expressed deep shame for the ouburst.)
With that letter, Rock Against Racism was born. “The idea was that if we harnessed music and politics together, it might be a powerful combination to fight fascism and racism.” Music was the key, to get the youth on board. The first event was a gig with jazz singer Carol Grimes at a pub in Forest Gate, east London. “We chose the Princess Alice because it was in an area where the National Front were getting substantial votes in local elections,” says Saunders. He admits they were anxious about getting attacked by the NF or the violent neo-Nazis of the British Movement, so they got a bunch of dockers in as security.
In the end, it passed off without incident, apart from the usual disagreement with the pub over money. Rock Against Racism grew and grew from there, fighting racism through live music and putting black and white bands on stage throughout the country. Saunders remembers one gig especially, at the Polytechnic of Central London, featuring the reggae band Misty in Roots and the punk band Sham 69, a lot of whose fans were skinheads. In fact, Saunders says, although the band’s frontman Jimmy Pursey was strongly opposed to far-right politics, some people around the band were members of the British Movement.
Saunders remembers the tension backstage. “Misty had a reading of the King James Bible, while getting into the mood of their music and culture. And they played dominoes, in the most theatrically aggressive way, slapping down the dominoes hard, all directed at these fascists and skinheads standing around watching. It was electric, I thought at any second it was going to kick off.” Somehow the gunslinger tactics defused the situation and the gig ended with the two bands on stage together in a show of solidarity.
The gigs grew into full-scale carnivals, most famously one in London’s Victoria Park featuring the Clash, Steel Pulse, the Tom Robinson Band and more; it began as a march from Trafalgar Square and is thought to have been attended by 100,000 people. But the movement was just as much about small, grassroots responses around the country. Saunders remembers hearing from a kid in Aberystwyth. “She said she’d read my letter in the music press, and that one of her teachers was a Nazi, what could she do? I wrote back and said: ‘You are now Rock Against Racism Aberystwyth.’ When we next heard from her, she’d set up a club – all the local punk bands were playing.”
Saunders says the far right today, with their black balaclava brigades, are more frightening than ever. “The hypocrisy – saying they’re looking after women and children, then we find out many have been reported to police for domestic abuse.” His rallying cry is to recognise the far right for what they want and who they are, and to call them out for it. “They’re looking to rid Britain of black and brown people. They’re flat-out, 100% racists.”
‘Our football tournament was huge. Peter Cook came down and refereed’
You could say that in 1977 the NF and Tottenham Hotspur FC were heading in opposite directions. The NF, led by John Tyndall, was still on the rise, resurgent in elections for the Greater London Council. Spurs, meanwhile, were relegated to the old second division; the terraces at White Hart Lane weren’t a happy place. “When the team is doing bad, the community does bad,” says fan Richard Buckwell, who was in his mid-20s at the time, and is speaking to me today on a video call from Nottingham, where he now lives.
The NF campaigned and recruited in and around football. “I suppose it’s historically the leading leisure activity of white men,” says Buckwell. When Spurs were back on the up and signed the Argentinians Ossie Ardiles and Ricky Villa, there was a lot animosity. Buckwell, who was active with the Anti Nazi League, and a few like-minded supporters, felt the opposite. “We handed out leaflets that said, ‘They’re welcome here’. And that’s what kicked off Spurs Against Nazis.”
It was launched with a public meeting, attended by about 60 people. In October 1978, they organised a five-a-side football tournament. “It was a huge event – we got 47 teams entering. Aswad participated, Bill Oddie played, Peter Cook came down and refereed.” Having the comedian Cook, a high-profile Spurs supporter, involved was helpful when the club initially tried to stop the use of its cockerel logo.
They printed T-shirts, made badges and banners, and handed out leaflets on match days, sometimes as the NF were doing the same. “I remember one day, leafleting outside the ground, suddenly seeing a load of youngsters running towards us. I thought, what on earth is happening? Is this the National Front?” But it was the opposite: they ran past to charge at and chase off the NF, who were campaigning behind. The message was getting across.
And the Football Fans Against Nazis message spread to other clubs: Leyton Orient, West Brom, Everton, Swansea City, Norwich, Arsenal. In all, about 11 clubs formed grassroots anti-fascist groups to counter the far-right infiltration of fanbases. The message even travelled abroad. “Some of our T-shirts got sent to the freedom fighters against white minority rule in what was then Rhodesia.” Buckwell still has a Spurs Against Nazis T-shirt, “for memory’s sake”. We’re joined on the call not by a Zimbabwean freedom fighter but by Buckwell’s wife, Jane, holding up this last surviving shirt. Plus, a nice cartoon of a footballer kicking a skinhead wearing an NF shirt into touch.
Buckwell remembers that when they saw NF graffiti, they used to alter it to read NF = No Fun. He says that anti-fascist campaigning – including by football fans – undoubtedly played a major part in the NF’s decline, though Tyndall and other members took its embers to ignite a new far-right flame in the British National party (BNP). Racism continued to rage, largely unchecked, through the football terraces, throughout the 80s.
And to this day it hasn’t been totally extinguished. “One thing that made a difference recently was taking the knee, which many clubs continued for a long time. And [former England manager] Gareth Southgate had a tremendous influence.” But campaigns, such as Kick It Out and Show Racism the Red Card, are underfunded, and he would like to see more support, from government and – particularly – from the clubs themselves. “They pay lip service. The amount of money swilling around the big clubs, they could do a lot more.”
At 74, Buckwell still fights the far right, working with Stand Up To Racism in Nottingham. He worries about Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (who goes by the name Tommy Robinson) and his lot. “It is frightening at the moment. But I went on the Together Alliance march, which was tremendous. Nottingham is very diverse and multicultural.”
‘I was stood in the middle of this room watching this horrific violence – this wasn’t the change I wanted’
On a summer evening in 1989, at what became known as the Battle of Welling, Matthew Collins changed sides. As a “troubled and troublesome youth” growing up in south-east London, he’d joined the NF as a teenager. “I was horrendously and viciously racist. I didn’t like what I saw around me.” He became the NF’s south London organiser.
In the mid-80s, the NF was becoming splintered and disorganised and Collins was also volunteering with the emerging BNP, rising to become its south London chair. The BNP opened a bookshop in Welling to distribute far-right material, and a group of concerned locals held a meeting at the library to discuss what to do about it.
Forty neo-Nazis – including Collins – stormed the building and attacked them. It was, he remembers, a bloodbath. Nine people were hospitalised. Most people at the meeting were women, of south Asian heritage. “I was stood in the middle of this room watching this horrific violence, people assaulting women in a library, and realised I’d been looking in the wrong places – this wasn’t the change I wanted.” Sickened, the following day he phoned the anti-fascist magazine Searchlight, and told them who had been involved. Collins had flipped; he was now an informant.
Over the next two and a half years or so, he continued his far-right activities but reported back to Searchlight, building up intelligence, warning of attacks, identifying people. It was incredibly stressful, and he would have been killed if he’d been found out, “particularly towards the end when Combat 18 [the security wing of the BNP] were around and it was all about shipping guns and drugs”. And he couldn’t tell anyone, not his family, not his girlfriend. “It was impossible, because you still have to live that life as a race hater.”
Collins took part in a World In Action TV exposé of Combat 18, blacked out and with his voice replaced, but because of what he said it still placed him in the firing line. When he got a visit from special branch, telling him they had intel that there was a threat against him, it was time to get out. Collins went to Australia for 10 years, where he worked in the rag trade and got married.
Now 54, Collins is back in the UK, working for Hope Not Hate, the advocacy group that campaigns against fascism and was an offshoot of Searchlight. He’s head of intelligence, meaning he now runs informants inside extreme organisations. He ran Robbie Mullen, the whistleblower who helped bring down extreme rightwing group National Action, a member of which was plotting to kill then Labour MP Rosie Cooper, and the subject of ITV drama The Walk-In (Stephen Graham played Collins).
He’s not going to tell me all the tricks of the trade, but basically they identify people who are disappointed and disaffected. “They have constant schisms and fallouts because the far right in this country is now completely driven by drugs and alcohol. You just pick and choose and you find someone and you put pressure on them.”
Collins wants to smash today’s far right. “Destroy, disorganise and disorientate. And one of the ways I do that is by finding the better-quality people and getting them out. We’re putting better-equipped and better-behaved people back into society.”
He divides the misery caused by the far right into two: “The misery of being in hock to them, ideologically, socially, culturally. And the misery of the people who live in fear of them, because they might get their windows broken or get beaten up.”
‘I was really proud of what we delivered, keeping them out, squashing them’
In the run-up to the 2010 general election, the far right were moving in on Jen Craft’s patch. “There were these, essentially, fascists not far from my home town and I wanted to do everything I could to stop them.”
Fortunately, she was in a position to do so. Craft (pictured page 23), born and raised in Thurrock in Essex, was working for the Labour MP, now peer, Margaret Hodge at the time, in Barking. The BNP had targeted the east London constituency as somewhere they could win. They’d done well there in the 2005 general election, and gained 12 council seats the following year.
Craft explains there was a lot of frustration in the area over lack of housing, drastically fewer jobs available with Ford in Dagenham, and rapid demographic change – from predominantly white working class to a significantly more mixed population. “It was a proper tinderbox.” A complacent local Labour party and council meant people “didn’t feel they had the ability to contact anyone or that politicians were on their side”.
The BNP were cleverer than the NF before them. “The way they approached people, they didn’t knock on your door and say, ‘You don’t like all these so-and-so people moving in, do you?’ They’d say, ‘That playground in the park looks a bit rundown, we’ll come and paint it. I bet you’ve not seen a politician in years, tell us what’s worrying you.’”
Craft, whose formative years had coincided with a Blair government and who saw herself as significantly left of him, knew what the BNP were all about. She believes they were targeting Hodge personally, “because she’s Jewish, and because she’d just lost her husband. They thought they could capitalise.”
Craft, who was 25 in 2010, ran Hodge’s campaign. “If you’re going to throw everything at defeating the far right, that’s a good time to do it – when you’ve no real responsibilities and can spend 80 hours a week going for it.”
How do you go about it? “If you knock on someone’s door and find they’re voting for the BNP and you say, ‘Did you know they’re a bunch of racists?’, what that person hears is you’re calling them a racist.” Nor did they begin with, “Hi, I’m from Labour … ” because, such was the mistrust, they would often end up with the door slammed in their faces. So they adopted tactics not unlike those of their opponents. “It was, ‘I’m out with your local team, what issues have you got, what can we fix? Not trying to convince them that our way of seeing the world is right, but just to open that door by saying, ‘We’re here, we’re listening, we’re on your side, how can we deliver for you?’” They organised coffee afternoons and street meetings to find out what it was people cared about.
Later, there was a bit of “Do you know who the BNP are?” And that was the approach in recruiting volunteers and building a campaign team. “This is who they are, this is the threat they pose, come and help us, because if they do win here, where are they going to go next? They won’t stop … ”
The BNP didn’t win. Though Labour lost nationally, in Barking Hodge increased her share of the vote, and the BNP were pushed into third place. It was a turning point for their support; the party fragmented, losing members to new parties emerging on the right, such as Ukip. “I was really proud of what we delivered, keeping them out, squashing them,” says Craft.
After that, she became a civil servant, and took a break from politics for a while. In 2024, she stood for Labour in Thurrock, and won. Now an MP, we’re talking in her Westminster office. The incumbent Tory was beaten into third place, behind Reform’s candidate.
The same issues – migration, economic uncertainty and insecurity, disaffection with politics – mean that “in my area, those far-right messages are taking hold again”. The difference now is social media. “In Barking, it was analogue – letters, leaflets. We just had to have a faster printer than theirs, more things to put through doors and more boots on the ground. But the advent of social media means people can spread untruths and distortions very, very quickly – like net migration is rising or there are more small boat crossings, when actually it’s the opposite.”
Craft thinks that to fight the far right today, what’s mostly needed is more regulation of social media companies, and their owners. “Elon Musk wants us to turn against and fight one another. The fact we are not regulating against him is stepping away from our duty to keep this country safe.”
That’s going to be more effective than some tactics she sees. “If you go with a placard and shout, ‘Nazis!’, you probably feel good about yourself, but you’ve done nothing to fight them where it counts, which is at the ballot box.”
‘You’ve heard of the concept of breaking bread and the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach … ’
In the summer of 2024, after the murder of three girls at a dance class in Southport, misinformation and violence spread across the UK. Mobs smashed windows and cars, attempted to set fire to hotels housing asylum seekers and desecrated Muslim graves, while far-right keyboard warriors poured petrol on the flames from their sunloungers abroad.
On the night of 2 August in Liverpool, an angry crowd gathered outside the Abdullah Quilliam mosque, the oldest in the country. Against police advice, Adam Kelwick, one of the imams, crossed the road to talk to them. He took food – burgers and chips – and drinks. “You’ve heard of the concept of breaking bread and the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach,” Kelwick says, on the phone from his Liverpool home. There is a famous picture of Kelwick talking to one man in particular. “I spoke to him for five minutes, we connected, built some kind of relationship, call it a friendship if you like, then I gave the guy a hug.”
It takes two to hug. “So he had it inside him. After coming to the mosque to protest, he could reach out and hug me as well – the same people he was manifesting enmity towards.” Later, when it had quietened down and the cameras had gone, Kelwick sneaked him into the mosque. “I took him in, we walked around, and had an interesting conversation.”
Kelwick thinks “the vast majority of people you see at these protests are just genuine, regular people who’ve been dragged into something they might not understand fully”. Which is why conversation is important. “You have to engage, otherwise you’ll go further apart, then it’s easy to hold enmity and hostility.”
Since that time, Kelwick has been devoting energy to building these links. He tells me about a coach trip they had to north Wales soon afterwards – a bunch of families who’d attended the Liverpool Save Our Kids protest, which kicked off violently, along with families from the Muslim community. “We mixed everyone up together on two coaches; you should have seen the looks on the faces of the locals in north Wales when the doors opened and all these scousers got off along with some quite conservative-looking Muslim families. I think the academics call it contact theory – that you’re less likely to have negative feelings towards each other or uphold negative stereotypes if you have in-person interaction.”
The paranoia cuts both ways. “A lot of people in the Muslim community think everyone at these protests wants to hang, draw and quarter them – so I’ve been working with both sides.”
Kelwick travels a lot, and says the narrative – pushed and funded from above by far-right campaigns and individuals – is the same everywhere: “Immigration is bad, it’s an invasion of military-aged men, they don’t integrate, they’re committing all these crimes and raping our girls … it’s the same in the US, France, Germany, all across Europe.”
But Kelwick has faith in people. “We’re all human, bleed the same blood, have the same issues in life. It doesn’t matter how many billions are pumped into this, if you can facilitate genuine interactions between people from different communities, that has the ability to make these hugely funded efforts irrelevant.”
Would he sit down for a chat with Tommy Robinson himself, I wonder? “It’s not a definite no. I almost arranged to visit him when he was in prison. I think that would be the ideal meeting, without cameras, without anything to prove to anybody, just a genuine sit down where we don’t have to pull any publicity stunt – that would be beneficial.”
Discussion rather than debate is the aim. “I don’t like to be the attacker; it pushes people away. The whole purpose of having this interaction is to come closer. When you strip things down to a human level, that’s where beautiful things can happen. You can do that with every single person – even Tommy Robinson.” Over to you, Mr Yaxley-Lennon, the invitation is there. There might even be a hug in it for you.

It’s not one organisation, it’s a mass movement.”
I think it’s likely those kids used another word for “black people” but I can’t quite find the stomach to ask. Mehmood is speaking to me on a video call from Beirut, where he teaches at the American University. Now 70, he migrated, in 1967, from Pakistan to Bradford, where his grandfather and uncles worked in the textile mills, and immediately experienced racism. “The headmaster would tell us to be grateful to be in England, we were beaten up by white boys on the way to school, there was an intense violence and a feeling of helplessness.”
Until he realised he wasn’t helpless, or alone. “We knew we couldn’t come to school on our own, so we assembled somewhere, got off the bus together and walked together to the classroom.”
Later, when he was himself working in a mill in Otley in the late 70s, Mehmood was one of the founders of the Bradford Asian Youth Movement. The AYMs were a network of anti-racist groups demanding equal rights and a fairer world as well as defending their communities against attacks from groups such as the National Front (NF) and the British Movement (BM).
Following disagreements within the AYM, Mehmood was part of a splinter group, the United Black Youth League, that broke away in 1981. “The police tried to paint that our split was because the UBYL wanted violence, but this is anything but the truth,” he says. “Some wanted to work within the system – one of the founders of the AYM became an MP, something I fundamentally disagreed with then as I do now.”
There were frequent attacks on the south Asian community in Bradford. “Whenever the National Front had a demonstration, you could always bet that after the pubs closed they would attack us, groups of skinheads – five, six, seven of them in a car, going around, seeing what they could do.”
So, as Mehmood had done at school, the UBYL organised themselves. “If you’re not organised, you get picked on. When you’re organised, often they will flee and you don’t have to fight. We couldn’t trust the police; either they were incapable, or they didn’t care, or they harassed us.”
When they learned that a lot of fascists were planning to go to Bradford, they got ready. “We mobilised hundreds, many of them white, walking around, making sure people knew we were out, they didn’t have anything to fear. We said we’d arm ourselves if need be. Some of us made petrol bombs.”
The petrol bombs require some context. “Remember, it was the year of the massacre of the teenagers in London,” he says, referring to the New Cross house fire in which 13 young black people died (even though it was never proved to have been a racist attack). “Members of the UBYL were blocking up their own letter boxes in case someone poured petrol in and set fire to their houses. That was a reality, and we said no, we will defend ourselves.”
In summer 1981, 12 members of the UBYL, including Mehmood, were arrested after a police raid discovered 38 milk bottles filled with petrol. The Bradford 12, as they became known, were charged with conspiracy to cause explosions and endanger lives. They didn’t deny making the molotov cocktails, but said it was a precaution for self-defence.
In jail, awaiting trial, Mehmood discovered another weapon: the pen. He wrote his first novel, Hand on the Sun, about a young immigrant experiencing racism. “Stories make us human. I wanted to share with future generations that we were proud industrial workers, we weren’t just going to have crumbs, we were politically conscious and had hope. I still have that hope.” After an active campaign and a lengthy trial, on 16 June 1982 Mehmood and the rest of the Bradford 12 – who had argued self-defence – were acquitted by a jury.
The situation with the far right is no better today, he says. In fact, the opposite: “The atmosphere is more vicious than it was in the 80s, primarily because we were dealing with old-style racism born out of British colonial history. Today’s Islamophobia is a more violent, virulent form; it has always been there, under the surface, since the Crusades, but not at a scale you see today. The far right at that time were a few thousand demonstrators here and there, not 100,000, half a million. And they’re not just in Britain, but across Europe.”
He sees it as a failure of the left, of the labour and trade union movements, to educate the white working class that “the real enemy is the billionaires at the top”. Plus, the loss of community organisations. Mehmood’s message about what to do about the far right today is to do as they did: organise and fight back. “The most important lesson is that if you believe there is an injustice, then fight against it.”
Tariq Mehmood’s memoir, Rebellion: Self-defence and the Story of the Bradford 12, is published by Daraja Press. A documentary, also titled Rebellion and co-directed by Mehmood, premieres at the BFI London film festival on October 14 and 15
‘The idea was to harness music and politics together to fight fascism and racism’
It was half a century ago, the hot summer of 1976, but Red Saunders remembers it clearly. A photographer and at the time also a member of a radical theatre group, he was in a rehearsal at a studio in Soho, London. “Someone came in and said: ‘Have you seen this shit about Eric Clapton?’”
An article in a music magazine said that at a concert in Birmingham, the musician had told his audience to vote for Enoch “rivers of blood” Powell in order to stop Britain from becoming “a black colony”, as well as chanting the NF slogan: Keep Britain White.
“I was a Clapton fan, I’d been to his gigs, had the albums. I couldn’t believe it,” says Saunders, now 80 and talking to me from his Suffolk home. He wrote a letter to the music press, and got some of his like-minded friends, including Roger Huddle and Jo Wreford to sign it. The letter pointed out Clapton’s hypocrisy, that he was “rock music’s biggest colonialist” and that his own music had its roots in blues, R&B, reggae. And it concluded with a rallying call for musicians and fans to rise up: “Keep the faith, black and white unite and fight.” (Clapton later apologised and expressed deep shame for the ouburst.)
With that letter, Rock Against Racism was born. “The idea was that if we harnessed music and politics together, it might be a powerful combination to fight fascism and racism.” Music was the key, to get the youth on board. The first event was a gig with jazz singer Carol Grimes at a pub in Forest Gate, east London. “We chose the Princess Alice because it was in an area where the National Front were getting substantial votes in local elections,” says Saunders. He admits they were anxious about getting attacked by the NF or the violent neo-Nazis of the British Movement, so they got a bunch of dockers in as security.
In the end, it passed off without incident, apart from the usual disagreement with the pub over money. Rock Against Racism grew and grew from there, fighting racism through live music and putting black and white bands on stage throughout the country. Saunders remembers one gig especially, at the Polytechnic of Central London, featuring the reggae band Misty in Roots and the punk band Sham 69, a lot of whose fans were skinheads. In fact, Saunders says, although the band’s frontman Jimmy Pursey was strongly opposed to far-right politics, some people around the band were members of the British Movement.
Saunders remembers the tension backstage. “Misty had a reading of the King James Bible, while getting into the mood of their music and culture. And they played dominoes, in the most theatrically aggressive way, slapping down the dominoes hard, all directed at these fascists and skinheads standing around watching. It was electric, I thought at any second it was going to kick off.” Somehow the gunslinger tactics defused the situation and the gig ended with the two bands on stage together in a show of solidarity.
The gigs grew into full-scale carnivals, most famously one in London’s Victoria Park featuring the Clash, Steel Pulse, the Tom Robinson Band and more; it began as a march from Trafalgar Square and is thought to have been attended by 100,000 people. But the movement was just as much about small, grassroots responses around the country. Saunders remembers hearing from a kid in Aberystwyth. “She said she’d read my letter in the music press, and that one of her teachers was a Nazi, what could she do? I wrote back and said: ‘You are now Rock Against Racism Aberystwyth.’ When we next heard from her, she’d set up a club – all the local punk bands were playing.”
Saunders says the far right today, with their black balaclava brigades, are more frightening than ever. “The hypocrisy – saying they’re looking after women and children, then we find out many have been reported to police for domestic abuse.” His rallying cry is to recognise the far right for what they want and who they are, and to call them out for it. “They’re looking to rid Britain of black and brown people. They’re flat-out, 100% racists.”
‘Our football tournament was huge. Peter Cook came down and refereed’
You could say that in 1977 the NF and Tottenham Hotspur FC were heading in opposite directions. The NF, led by John Tyndall, was still on the rise, resurgent in elections for the Greater London Council. Spurs, meanwhile, were relegated to the old second division; the terraces at White Hart Lane weren’t a happy place. “When the team is doing bad, the community does bad,” says fan Richard Buckwell, who was in his mid-20s at the time, and is speaking to me today on a video call from Nottingham, where he now lives.
The NF campaigned and recruited in and around football. “I suppose it’s historically the leading leisure activity of white men,” says Buckwell. When Spurs were back on the up and signed the Argentinians Ossie Ardiles and Ricky Villa, there was a lot animosity. Buckwell, who was active with the Anti Nazi League, and a few like-minded supporters, felt the opposite. “We handed out leaflets that said, ‘They’re welcome here’. And that’s what kicked off Spurs Against Nazis.”
It was launched with a public meeting, attended by about 60 people. In October 1978, they organised a five-a-side football tournament. “It was a huge event – we got 47 teams entering. Aswad participated, Bill Oddie played, Peter Cook came down and refereed.” Having the comedian Cook, a high-profile Spurs supporter, involved was helpful when the club initially tried to stop the use of its cockerel logo.
They printed T-shirts, made badges and banners, and handed out leaflets on match days, sometimes as the NF were doing the same. “I remember one day, leafleting outside the ground, suddenly seeing a load of youngsters running towards us. I thought, what on earth is happening? Is this the National Front?” But it was the opposite: they ran past to charge at and chase off the NF, who were campaigning behind. The message was getting across.
And the Football Fans Against Nazis message spread to other clubs: Leyton Orient, West Brom, Everton, Swansea City, Norwich, Arsenal. In all, about 11 clubs formed grassroots anti-fascist groups to counter the far-right infiltration of fanbases. The message even travelled abroad. “Some of our T-shirts got sent to the freedom fighters against white minority rule in what was then Rhodesia.” Buckwell still has a Spurs Against Nazis T-shirt, “for memory’s sake”. We’re joined on the call not by a Zimbabwean freedom fighter but by Buckwell’s wife, Jane, holding up this last surviving shirt. Plus, a nice cartoon of a footballer kicking a skinhead wearing an NF shirt into touch.
Buckwell remembers that when they saw NF graffiti, they used to alter it to read NF = No Fun. He says that anti-fascist campaigning – including by football fans – undoubtedly played a major part in the NF’s decline, though Tyndall and other members took its embers to ignite a new far-right flame in the British National party (BNP). Racism continued to rage, largely unchecked, through the football terraces, throughout the 80s.
And to this day it hasn’t been totally extinguished. “One thing that made a difference recently was taking the knee, which many clubs continued for a long time. And [former England manager] Gareth Southgate had a tremendous influence.” But campaigns, such as Kick It Out and Show Racism the Red Card, are underfunded, and he would like to see more support, from government and – particularly – from the clubs themselves. “They pay lip service. The amount of money swilling around the big clubs, they could do a lot more.”
At 74, Buckwell still fights the far right, working with Stand Up To Racism in Nottingham. He worries about Stephen Yaxley-Lennon (who goes by the name Tommy Robinson) and his lot. “It is frightening at the moment. But I went on the Together Alliance march, which was tremendous. Nottingham is very diverse and multicultural.”
‘I was stood in the middle of this room watching this horrific violence – this wasn’t the change I wanted’
On a summer evening in 1989, at what became known as the Battle of Welling, Matthew Collins changed sides. As a “troubled and troublesome youth” growing up in south-east London, he’d joined the NF as a teenager. “I was horrendously and viciously racist. I didn’t like what I saw around me.” He became the NF’s south London organiser.
In the mid-80s, the NF was becoming splintered and disorganised and Collins was also volunteering with the emerging BNP, rising to become its south London chair. The BNP opened a bookshop in Welling to distribute far-right material, and a group of concerned locals held a meeting at the library to discuss what to do about it.
Forty neo-Nazis – including Collins – stormed the building and attacked them. It was, he remembers, a bloodbath. Nine people were hospitalised. Most people at the meeting were women, of south Asian heritage. “I was stood in the middle of this room watching this horrific violence, people assaulting women in a library, and realised I’d been looking in the wrong places – this wasn’t the change I wanted.” Sickened, the following day he phoned the anti-fascist magazine Searchlight, and told them who had been involved. Collins had flipped; he was now an informant.
Over the next two and a half years or so, he continued his far-right activities but reported back to Searchlight, building up intelligence, warning of attacks, identifying people. It was incredibly stressful, and he would have been killed if he’d been found out, “particularly towards the end when Combat 18 [the security wing of the BNP] were around and it was all about shipping guns and drugs”. And he couldn’t tell anyone, not his family, not his girlfriend. “It was impossible, because you still have to live that life as a race hater.”
Collins took part in a World In Action TV exposé of Combat 18, blacked out and with his voice replaced, but because of what he said it still placed him in the firing line. When he got a visit from special branch, telling him they had intel that there was a threat against him, it was time to get out. Collins went to Australia for 10 years, where he worked in the rag trade and got married.
Now 54, Collins is back in the UK, working for Hope Not Hate, the advocacy group that campaigns against fascism and was an offshoot of Searchlight. He’s head of intelligence, meaning he now runs informants inside extreme organisations. He ran Robbie Mullen, the whistleblower who helped bring down extreme rightwing group National Action, a member of which was plotting to kill then Labour MP Rosie Cooper, and the subject of ITV drama The Walk-In (Stephen Graham played Collins).
He’s not going to tell me all the tricks of the trade, but basically they identify people who are disappointed and disaffected. “They have constant schisms and fallouts because the far right in this country is now completely driven by drugs and alcohol. You just pick and choose and you find someone and you put pressure on them.”
Collins wants to smash today’s far right. “Destroy, disorganise and disorientate. And one of the ways I do that is by finding the better-quality people and getting them out. We’re putting better-equipped and better-behaved people back into society.”
He divides the misery caused by the far right into two: “The misery of being in hock to them, ideologically, socially, culturally. And the misery of the people who live in fear of them, because they might get their windows broken or get beaten up.”
‘I was really proud of what we delivered, keeping them out, squashing them’
In the run-up to the 2010 general election, the far right were moving in on Jen Craft’s patch. “There were these, essentially, fascists not far from my home town and I wanted to do everything I could to stop them.”
Fortunately, she was in a position to do so. Craft (pictured page 23), born and raised in Thurrock in Essex, was working for the Labour MP, now peer, Margaret Hodge at the time, in Barking. The BNP had targeted the east London constituency as somewhere they could win. They’d done well there in the 2005 general election, and gained 12 council seats the following year.
Craft explains there was a lot of frustration in the area over lack of housing, drastically fewer jobs available with Ford in Dagenham, and rapid demographic change – from predominantly white working class to a significantly more mixed population. “It was a proper tinderbox.” A complacent local Labour party and council meant people “didn’t feel they had the ability to contact anyone or that politicians were on their side”.
The BNP were cleverer than the NF before them. “The way they approached people, they didn’t knock on your door and say, ‘You don’t like all these so-and-so people moving in, do you?’ They’d say, ‘That playground in the park looks a bit rundown, we’ll come and paint it. I bet you’ve not seen a politician in years, tell us what’s worrying you.’”
Craft, whose formative years had coincided with a Blair government and who saw herself as significantly left of him, knew what the BNP were all about. She believes they were targeting Hodge personally, “because she’s Jewish, and because she’d just lost her husband. They thought they could capitalise.”
Craft, who was 25 in 2010, ran Hodge’s campaign. “If you’re going to throw everything at defeating the far right, that’s a good time to do it – when you’ve no real responsibilities and can spend 80 hours a week going for it.”
How do you go about it? “If you knock on someone’s door and find they’re voting for the BNP and you say, ‘Did you know they’re a bunch of racists?’, what that person hears is you’re calling them a racist.” Nor did they begin with, “Hi, I’m from Labour … ” because, such was the mistrust, they would often end up with the door slammed in their faces. So they adopted tactics not unlike those of their opponents. “It was, ‘I’m out with your local team, what issues have you got, what can we fix? Not trying to convince them that our way of seeing the world is right, but just to open that door by saying, ‘We’re here, we’re listening, we’re on your side, how can we deliver for you?’” They organised coffee afternoons and street meetings to find out what it was people cared about.
Later, there was a bit of “Do you know who the BNP are?” And that was the approach in recruiting volunteers and building a campaign team. “This is who they are, this is the threat they pose, come and help us, because if they do win here, where are they going to go next? They won’t stop … ”
The BNP didn’t win. Though Labour lost nationally, in Barking Hodge increased her share of the vote, and the BNP were pushed into third place. It was a turning point for their support; the party fragmented, losing members to new parties emerging on the right, such as Ukip. “I was really proud of what we delivered, keeping them out, squashing them,” says Craft.
After that, she became a civil servant, and took a break from politics for a while. In 2024, she stood for Labour in Thurrock, and won. Now an MP, we’re talking in her Westminster office. The incumbent Tory was beaten into third place, behind Reform’s candidate.
The same issues – migration, economic uncertainty and insecurity, disaffection with politics – mean that “in my area, those far-right messages are taking hold again”. The difference now is social media. “In Barking, it was analogue – letters, leaflets. We just had to have a faster printer than theirs, more things to put through doors and more boots on the ground. But the advent of social media means people can spread untruths and distortions very, very quickly – like net migration is rising or there are more small boat crossings, when actually it’s the opposite.”
Craft thinks that to fight the far right today, what’s mostly needed is more regulation of social media companies, and their owners. “Elon Musk wants us to turn against and fight one another. The fact we are not regulating against him is stepping away from our duty to keep this country safe.”
That’s going to be more effective than some tactics she sees. “If you go with a placard and shout, ‘Nazis!’, you probably feel good about yourself, but you’ve done nothing to fight them where it counts, which is at the ballot box.”
‘You’ve heard of the concept of breaking bread and the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach … ’
In the summer of 2024, after the murder of three girls at a dance class in Southport, misinformation and violence spread across the UK. Mobs smashed windows and cars, attempted to set fire to hotels housing asylum seekers and desecrated Muslim graves, while far-right keyboard warriors poured petrol on the flames from their sunloungers abroad.
On the night of 2 August in Liverpool, an angry crowd gathered outside the Abdullah Quilliam mosque, the oldest in the country. Against police advice, Adam Kelwick, one of the imams, crossed the road to talk to them. He took food – burgers and chips – and drinks. “You’ve heard of the concept of breaking bread and the way to a man’s heart is through his stomach,” Kelwick says, on the phone from his Liverpool home. There is a famous picture of Kelwick talking to one man in particular. “I spoke to him for five minutes, we connected, built some kind of relationship, call it a friendship if you like, then I gave the guy a hug.”
It takes two to hug. “So he had it inside him. After coming to the mosque to protest, he could reach out and hug me as well – the same people he was manifesting enmity towards.” Later, when it had quietened down and the cameras had gone, Kelwick sneaked him into the mosque. “I took him in, we walked around, and had an interesting conversation.”
Kelwick thinks “the vast majority of people you see at these protests are just genuine, regular people who’ve been dragged into something they might not understand fully”. Which is why conversation is important. “You have to engage, otherwise you’ll go further apart, then it’s easy to hold enmity and hostility.”
Since that time, Kelwick has been devoting energy to building these links. He tells me about a coach trip they had to north Wales soon afterwards – a bunch of families who’d attended the Liverpool Save Our Kids protest, which kicked off violently, along with families from the Muslim community. “We mixed everyone up together on two coaches; you should have seen the looks on the faces of the locals in north Wales when the doors opened and all these scousers got off along with some quite conservative-looking Muslim families. I think the academics call it contact theory – that you’re less likely to have negative feelings towards each other or uphold negative stereotypes if you have in-person interaction.”
The paranoia cuts both ways. “A lot of people in the Muslim community think everyone at these protests wants to hang, draw and quarter them – so I’ve been working with both sides.”
Kelwick travels a lot, and says the narrative – pushed and funded from above by far-right campaigns and individuals – is the same everywhere: “Immigration is bad, it’s an invasion of military-aged men, they don’t integrate, they’re committing all these crimes and raping our girls … it’s the same in the US, France, Germany, all across Europe.”
But Kelwick has faith in people. “We’re all human, bleed the same blood, have the same issues in life. It doesn’t matter how many billions are pumped into this, if you can facilitate genuine interactions between people from different communities, that has the ability to make these hugely funded efforts irrelevant.”
Would he sit down for a chat with Tommy Robinson himself, I wonder? “It’s not a definite no. I almost arranged to visit him when he was in prison. I think that would be the ideal meeting, without cameras, without anything to prove to anybody, just a genuine sit down where we don’t have to pull any publicity stunt – that would be beneficial.”
Discussion rather than debate is the aim. “I don’t like to be the attacker; it pushes people away. The whole purpose of having this interaction is to come closer. When you strip things down to a human level, that’s where beautiful things can happen. You can do that with every single person – even Tommy Robinson.” Over to you, Mr Yaxley-Lennon, the invitation is there. There might even be a hug in it for you.

title: 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year
content_c:
'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year
October 10, 2026
The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.
The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.
"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.
It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.
Shortlist also included 'Peak' and 'Crashout'
"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."
All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.
Around one million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.
"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."
"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added. "It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment."
Peak crash out
"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.
But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.
As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."
PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.
"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.
This article was originally written in German.
description: Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

title: Weg frei für Koalitionsverhandlungen in Schwerin
content_c:
Grüne in MV machen Weg frei für Koalitionsverhandlungen
Auf einem kleinen Parteitag haben die Delegierten von Bündnis90/Die Grünen geschlossen für Verhandlungen mit SPD und Linken gestimmt. Diese sollen damit am Montag starten.
"Jetzt beginnt die Arbeit, für die die Grünen gewählt wurden", erklärte die neue Fraktionsvorsitzende Claudia Müller den Delegierten und warb um ihre Zustimmung, mit SPD und Linken über eine mögliche Koalition verhandeln zu können. Die Sondierungsgespräche seien intensiv gewesen, man habe dabei auch gemeinsam nach hinten geschaut: "Und ja, wir haben auch gemeinsam über Russland und Nord Stream gesprochen. Man kann sagen, wir haben uns ausgesprochen. In der Gruppe, aber auch ganz persönlich.", sagte Claudia Müller. Das sei eine wichtige Grundlage gewesen, für sie sei das Thema damit beendet.
Müller: "Rechtsextremismus größte Gefahr für Demokratie"
Die Partei müsse nun in unsicheren Zeiten Verantwortung übernehmen, auch für die Menschen im Land, die nicht SPD, Linke oder die Grünen gewählt haben, so Claudia Müller. Viele würden sich fragen, ob der Staat für sie noch funktioniere, deshalb gehe es jetzt nicht darum, was jede Partei bei den Verhandlungen raushole, sondern was das Land brauche. Rechtsextremismus sei dabei das größte Problem für die Demokratie. In einer gemeinsamen Erklärung hatten die Verhandlungsparteien gestern angekündigt, einen parlamentarischen Untersuchungsausschuss zu rechtsextremen Netzwerken im Land einrichten zu wollen.
Sorge um Verlust "grüner" Themen
Mit Blick auf das Sondierungspapier äußerten einige Parteimitglieder die Sorge, dass angesichts einer klammen Landeskasse nicht genug Geld da sein könnte für grüne Projekte. Auch ein Untersuchungsausschuss sei teuer. Anderen Mitgliedern fehlen bisher Vorschläge und Konzepte zum Thema Migration, sowie ein klares Bekenntnis zum Ausbau von erneuerbaren Energien. Eine Teilnehmerin erklärte auch, dass man Vertrauen von Wählerinnen und Wählern breche, wenn man nicht in eine Koalition gehe. Es sei ein Wahlversprechen der Grünen gewesen, eine stabile demokratische Mehrheit zu bilden. Der Antrag des Landesvorstandes für Koalitionsverhandlungen wurde schließlich von den 24 Delegierten einstimmig angenommen.
SPD und Linke stimmten Freitagabend für Verhandlungen
Damit haben auch die Bündnisgrünen den Weg für Koalitionsverhandlungen frei gemacht. Am Freitagabend hatten bereits die Landesvorstände von SPD und Linken dafür gestimmt. Die Verhandlungsteilnehmer aller drei Parteien machten deutlich, dass man nicht nur ein Bündnis aus drei Parteien sein wolle, sondern eine Koalition für alle Menschen im Land. Die Koalitionsverhandlungen sollen am Montagvormittag im Schweriner Schloss beginnen.
author: Carolin Kock
description: Nach SPD und Linken haben in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern auch die Grünen für Koalitionsverhandlungen zur Bildung einer rot-rot-grünen Landesregierung gestimmt. Die Koalitionsgespräche sollen am Montag beginnen.

title: Trump dreht Russlands Dieselhähne auf
content_c:
Trump dreht Russlands Dieselhähne auf
10. Oktober 2026
US-Präsident Donald Trump hat nach einem Gespräch mit Kremlchef Wladimir Putin die Lieferung großer Mengen an Diesel aus Russland in Aussicht gestellt. Mehr als 300.000 Tonnen des Treibstoffs stünden sofort für die Vereinigten Staaten und den Weltmarkt zur Verfügung, 500.000 weitere Tonnen folgten im November. Danach sollten zusätzlich mehrere Millionen Tonnen aus Russland exportiert werden, soweit die dortigen Kapazitäten es zuließen.
Dies werde die Spritpreise erheblich senken, schrieb Trump in sozialen Medien. Wenige Wochen vor den Zwischenwahlen im November stehen der Präsident und dessen republikanische Partei wegen stark gestiegener Spritpreise innenpolitisch unter Druck. Wegen des russischen Angriffskriegs gegen die Ukraine hatten die USA Sanktionen gegen Energieunternehmen in Russland verhängt, die nun zu Teilen ausgesetzt werden. Das US-Finanzministerium erteilte eine befristete Importgenehmigung bis Anfang April.
Selenskyj: "Unwürdig"
Der Kreml bestätigte die Vereinbarung und erklärte, man sei bereit, Erdöl und dessen Verarbeitungsprodukte in die Vereinigten Staaten und auf den Weltmarkt zu liefern. Das werde sich positiv auf die gesamte globale Wirtschaft auswirken. Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj kritisierte die "unwürdige" Übereinkunft hingegen scharf. Sie verschaffe Moskau zusätzliche Mittel für seine Kriegsführung und untergrabe die Bemühungen um eine Friedenslösung, erklärte er.
Nach Angaben der US-Energiebehörde EIA liegt der Verbrauch von Diesel und anderen Destillat-Kraftstoffen in den USA derzeit bei durchschnittlich rund 3,77 Millionen Barrel täglich. Das entspricht umgerechnet etwa 500.000 Tonnen. Eine Menge von 300.000 Tonnen würde damit rechnerisch den US-Verbrauch für gut 14 Stunden decken.
Experte: "Unbedeutend"
Mehrere Experten bezweifeln denn auch, dass die russischen Lieferungen einen nachhaltigen Preisrückgang zur Folge haben. "Ich kann gar nicht genug betonen, wie unbedeutend das ist", erklärte etwa der Öl-Analyst Rory Johnston. Die US-Terminkontrakte für Diesel gaben nach Bekanntwerden der Einigung dennoch um rund fünf Prozent auf 1,23 Dollar (1,10 Euro) pro Liter nach.
Die Dieselpreise, die als einer der maßgeblichen Treiber von Inflation gelten, sind seit Beginn des von den USA und Israel begonnenen Krieges gegen den Iran im Februar um 70 Prozent gestiegen. Die Konflikte im Nahen und Mittleren Osten und in der Ukraine haben weltweit zu einem Engpass bei der Kraftstoffversorgung geführt.
Während Russland bei seinen Attacken immer wieder auf die ukrainische Energieversorgung zielt, verstärkt die Ukraine seit einiger Zeit ihre Angriffe auf Objekte der Öl-Industrie in Russland. Da viele russische Raffinerien beschädigt sind, hat sich die dortige Dieselproduktion von ursprünglich sieben Millionen Tonnen im Monat ungefähr halbiert.
jj/pgr (dpa, afp, rtr)
description: Der US-Präsident und sein russischer Counterpart, Kremlchef Putin, schließen eine Vereinbarung, die beiden nützen soll: Trump könnte sie Stimmen bringen, Putin Geld. Die Ukraine sieht sich als benachteiligter Dritter.

title: На фронті майже 200 боїв за день, найбільше на трьох напрямках – Генштаб
content_c:
На фронті майже 200 боїв за день, найбільше на трьох напрямках – Генштаб
На фронті від початку доби відбулося 195 бойових зіткнень, зокрема на Покровському напрямку зафіксовано 20 атак, на Гуляйпільському – 18, на Костянтинівському – 15.
Джерело: зведення Генштабу ЗСУ станом на 22:00
Деталі: На Північно-Слобожанському і Курському напрямках Сили оборони відбили три штурмові дії противника. Агресор завдав трьох авіаційних ударів із застосуванням семи КАБ та здійснив 131 обстріл позицій українських військ і населених пунктів, один з яких – із застосуванням РСЗВ.
На Південно-Слобожанському напрямку противник дев'ять разів атакував позиції українських підрозділів біля населених пунктів Стариця, Вовчанськ, Вовчанські Хутори та в бік Радьківки.
На Куп'янському напрямку зафіксовано одне боєзіткнення в районі Нової Кругляківки.
На Лиманському напрямку оборонці зупинили сім спроб росіян просунутися вперед в районах населених пунктів Надія, Новоєгорівка, Новоселівка, Лиман та Діброва.
На Слов'янському напрямку Сили оборони відбили три атаки ворога поблизу Озерного, Кривої Луки та в бік Пискунівки, ще одне боєзіткнення триває.
На Костянтинівському напрямку зафіксовано 15 бойових зіткнень у районах Костянтинівки, Новоселівки, Вільного та в напрямку населених пунктів Миколайпілля, Райське, одна атака триває.
На Покровському напрямку зафіксовано 20 атак у районах населених пунктів Світле, Молодецьке, Новомиколаївка та в бік Добропілля, Сергіївки.
На Гуляйпільському напрямку зафіксовано 18 російських атак у районах Рибного, Верхньої Терси, Гуляйпільського, Малої Токмачки та в бік населених пунктів Косівцеве, Нове Запоріжжя, Рівне, Воздвижівка, Копані.
На Придніпровському напрямку оборонці успішно зупинили одну атаку РФ.
author: Катерина Тищенко
description: Сили оборони стримують атаки на Покровському, Гуляйпільському та Костянтинівському напрямках, всього за день – 195 боєзіткнень.

title: Фрау ненависть. Хто така Аліса Вайдель і як вона стала найпопулярнішим ультраправим політиком Німеччини з часів Гітлера
content_c:
Фрау ненависть. Хто така Аліса Вайдель і як вона стала найпопулярнішим ультраправим політиком Німеччини з часів Гітлера
«Це не наша війна», — каже Вайдель про повномасштабне вторгнення Росії в Україну і закликає припинити допомогу Києву (Фото: REUTERS/Lisi Niesner)
Канцлер Німеччини Фрідріх Мерц переживає найважчий час у своїй політичній кар'єрі. Майже 60% німців схвалили б його відставку, а підтримка правлячої партії ХДС знизилася до історичного мінімуму у 18%. На руїнах рейтингу політсили Мерца приголомшливого прориву досягла проросійська ультраправа Альтернатива для Німеччини (AfD), яку співочолює Аліса Вайдель — одна з найодіозніших і водночас найзагадковіших політикинь у Німеччині.
AfD стала першою ультраправою партією у ФРН після Другої світової війни, яка вирвалася в лідери загальнонімецьких соцопитувань і наростила рейтинг до 30%. Її поступ лише міцніє. У 2024 році AfD вперше з часів нацистської Німеччини отримала високе крісло у виконавчій владі, коли її представник очолив округ у Тюрингії. На федеральних виборах 2025-го стала другою політсилою у Бундестазі і вдвічі збільшила підтримку (з 10% до 20%). У вересні 2026-го — перемогла на регіональних парламентських виборах у кількох східних землях, а в одній з них претендує на перше за 80 років крісло регіонального прем'єра для ультраправих.

title: Яке церковне свято в Україні 11 жовтня
content_c:
Яке церковне свято в Україні 11 жовтня
Що за церковне свято святкують в Україні за новим і старим календарем і кому моляться віряни — читайте в матеріалі ТСН.ua.
11 жовтня (24 жовтня), в православному календарі день пам’яті апостола Филипа, диякона. Филип жив у I столітті та належав до першої християнської громади в Єрусалимі. Його ім’я вперше згадується у шостому розділі «Діянь апостолів».
У той час кількість християн швидко зростала, і в громаді виникла суперечка через розподіл щоденної допомоги вдовам. Щоб апостоли могли більше часу присвячувати молитві та проповіді, громада обрала сімох чоловіків, яким доручили піклуватися про ці практичні справи.
Серед них були Стефан, Филип, Прохор, Никанор, Тимон, Пармен і Миколай з Антіохії. Саме цих сімох у християнській традиції часто вважають першими дияконами, хоча безпосередньо в цьому уривку «Діянь» вони так не названі.
Після обрання апостоли помолилися та поклали на них руки.
Після загибелі Стефана в Єрусалимі почалися переслідування християн. Багато вірян залишили місто й вирушили в інші місцевості. Серед них був і Филип.
Він прийшов до Самарії та почав проповідувати там Христа. Згідно з «Діяннями апостолів», його проповідь супроводжувалася зціленнями, а багато самарян прийняли хрещення.
Ця подія мала особливе значення для раннього християнства. Самаряни та юдеї мали давні релігійні суперечності, однак проповідь Филипа показала, що нова віра виходить за межі однієї громади чи народу.
Пізніше до Самарії прибули апостоли Петро та Іван.
Один із найвідоміших епізодів життя Филипа — його зустріч з ефіопським вельможею.
У «Діяннях апостолів» розповідається, що ангел Господній наказав Филипові вирушити на дорогу, яка вела з Єрусалима до Гази. Там він зустрів високопоставленого чиновника ефіопської цариці Кандакії, який повертався з Єрусалима та дорогою читав книгу пророка Ісаї.
Филип підійшов до його колісниці й запитав, чи розуміє той прочитане. Чоловік відповів, що потребує когось, хто пояснив би йому текст.
Тоді Филип розтлумачив уривок із книги Ісаї та розповів йому про Ісуса. Побачивши воду біля дороги, вельможа захотів охреститися. Филип здійснив хрещення, після чого, за біблійною розповіддю, Дух Господній забрав його звідти, а новонавернений продовжив свій шлях.
Цей епізод став одним із символів поширення християнства за межами Юдеї.
Церковне свято 11 жовтня — день пам’яті преподобного Теофана, єпископа Нікейського
Теофан народився в другій половині VIII століття. За церковним переданням, його батьків звали Іона та Анна. Вони дали синам Теофану та Феодору добру освіту й виховували їх у християнській вірі.
Брати обрали чернече життя і вступили до монастиря святого Сави Освяченого поблизу Єрусалима. Там Теофан присвятив себе молитві, вивченню Святого Письма та богослов’я.
Згодом він був висвячений на священника.
Життя Теофана припало на період іконоборства у Візантійській імперії. Прихильники цієї течії виступали проти релігійного шанування ікон, а імператорська влада в окремі періоди переслідувала тих, хто захищав їх використання у християнському богослужінні.
Єрусалимський патріарх направив Теофана та його брата Феодора до Константинополя, де вони мали виступити на захист шанування ікон.
Брати відкрито відстоювали свою позицію, через що зазнали переслідувань. Їх ув’язнювали, допитували та відправляли у заслання.
Однак навіть після цього вони не відмовилися від своїх переконань.
Особливо тяжкі переслідування припали на час правління візантійського імператора Феофіла, який був противником іконошанування.
За церковним житієм, Теофана та Феодора привели на суд, де від них вимагали відмовитися від захисту ікон. Після відмови братів жорстоко покарали.
На їхніх обличчях розпеченими голками або залізом, за різними версіями переказу, накреслили глузливі віршовані рядки. Саме через це братів почали називати Начертаними.
Це покарання мало не лише завдати фізичного болю, а й публічно принизити їх. Проте у християнській традиції воно, навпаки, стало символом їхньої стійкості.
Після катувань братів знову відправили у заслання.
Після відновлення іконошанування Теофан був поставлений єпископом Нікеї — одного з найважливіших християнських центрів Візантійської імперії.
Так людина, яка протягом багатьох років зазнавала переслідувань за свої релігійні переконання, стала очільником великої церковної громади.
На єпископській кафедрі Теофан продовжував служіння Церкві та займався літературною діяльністю.
Церковне свято в Україні 11 жовтня за старим календарем
За старим календарем 11 жовтня в Україні вшановують пам’ять преподобного Харитона Сповідника. За церковним переданням, Харитон постраждав під час гонінь на християн, однак залишився живим, тому отримав найменування Сповідника. Згодом він оселився в Палестині, де провадив суворе чернече життя та заснував кілька монастирів. Його вважають одним із засновників палестинського чернецтва.
Прикмети 11 жовтня
- Якщо зайці ще не змінили хутро на біле — зима прийде пізно.
- Птахи літають низько над землею — чекали на ранню та холодну зиму.
- Низько пливуть важкі хмари — незабаром похолодає.
Що не можна робити 11 жовтня
За давніми повір’ями, 11 жовтня не годиться проводити без справ і відкладати роботу на потім. Апостола Филипа в народній традиції пов’язували зі старанністю та допомогою ближнім, тому цього дня особливо засуджували ледарювання. Вірили, що пасивність може принести життєві негаразди, а занедбана й неприбрана оселя — стати перешкодою для добробуту та достатку в родині.
Що можна робити 11 жовтня
У народній традиції 11 жовтня відоме як Филипів день, адже цієї дати також вшановують пам’ять апостола Филипа. Здавна вважалося, що цього дня варто приділити увагу домашнім справам: навести лад у помешканні, перебрати речі та позбутися зайвого. Так господарі готували свою оселю до наближення холодів і намагалися увійти в зимовий період із чистим та впорядкованим домом.

За церковним переданням, Харитон постраждав під час гонінь на християн, однак залишився живим, тому отримав найменування Сповідника. Згодом він оселився в Палестині, де провадив суворе чернече життя та заснував кілька монастирів. Його вважають одним із засновників палестинського чернецтва.
Прикмети 11 жовтня
- Якщо зайці ще не змінили хутро на біле — зима прийде пізно.
- Птахи літають низько над землею — чекали на ранню та холодну зиму.
- Низько пливуть важкі хмари — незабаром похолодає.
Що не можна робити 11 жовтня
За давніми повір’ями, 11 жовтня не годиться проводити без справ і відкладати роботу на потім. Апостола Филипа в народній традиції пов’язували зі старанністю та допомогою ближнім, тому цього дня особливо засуджували ледарювання. Вірили, що пасивність може принести життєві негаразди, а занедбана й неприбрана оселя — стати перешкодою для добробуту та достатку в родині.
Що можна робити 11 жовтня
У народній традиції 11 жовтня відоме як Филипів день, адже цієї дати також вшановують пам’ять апостола Филипа. Здавна вважалося, що цього дня варто приділити увагу домашнім справам: навести лад у помешканні, перебрати речі та позбутися зайвого. Так господарі готували свою оселю до наближення холодів і намагалися увійти в зимовий період із чистим та впорядкованим домом.

title: ВОЗ не смогла установить причину смерти работницы российского противочумного института
content_c:
Всемирная организация здравоохранения (ВОЗ) заявила, что до сих пор не знает причину, вызвавшую смертельную пневмонию у сотрудницы российского противочумного института. Женщина скончалась 2 октября в Сибири, после чего около 200 человек поместили на карантин. Об этом сообщило информационное агентство Reuters.
ВОЗ 10 октября сообщила, что диагноз сотрудницы противочумного исследовательского центра в Сибири остаётся ею неподтверждённым. Организация также отметила, что случаев чумы ею не зарегистрировано. По информации российских СМИ, умершей была 28-летняя Дарья Шипилова, которая работала в Иркутском противочумном институте Сибири и Дальнего Востока.
Российский государственный регулятор передал ВОЗ результаты обследований умершей и людей, контактировавших с ней. Анализы на проверенные возбудители высокой опасности в предоставленных РФ результатах оказались отрицательными. У контактных лиц симптомов до сих пор нет. Новых случаев тяжелой пневмонии, связанных с этим событием, также не выявлено. Именно эти российские данные организация использовала для оценки ситуации.
«На основании предоставленной информации ВОЗ не обнаружила доказательств дальнейшего распространения инфекции, связанного с этим событием. Ключевой неопределенностью остается отсутствие подтвержденного диагноза у умершей сотрудницы лаборатории», — говорится в заявлении организации.
Работница заболела и скончалась 2 октября при обстоятельствах, подробности которых не обнародовались. После её смерти российские власти ввели карантин примерно для 200 человек. Сообщения об этом событии вызвали в социальных сетях беспокойство относительно угрозы здоровью населения. Неустановленная причина заболевания остаётся основным вопросом и после проведённых обследований.
После пандемии COVID-19 международные специалисты в области здравоохранения уделяют особое внимание смертельным случаям пневмонии неизвестного происхождения. Пандемия началась с группы случаев респираторного заболевания в Китае, которое быстро распространялось и приводило к летальным исходам. В то же время причину отдельных случаев пневмонии часто не удается установить. Сам по себе неподтвержденный диагноз не объясняет, какой именно возбудитель мог вызвать болезнь сотрудницы института.
Российские власти заявили, что женщина имела все необходимые прививки. По их данным, в организме умершей не обнаружили микроорганизмов, связанных с её профессиональной деятельностью. В четверг, 8 октября, Россия сообщила о завершении медицинских обследований всех контактных лиц. Власти РФ также утверждают, что передали ВОЗ полную информацию в соответствии с установленными процедурами.
Напомним, что в МИД Украины заявили об отсутствии выявленных угроз для страны на фоне сообщений о возможной вспышке чумы в России. Пресс-секретарь ведомства Георгий Тихий сообщил, что украинские компетентные органы и система здравоохранения внимательно следят за ситуацией. Тихий обвинил российские власти в сокрытии масштабов и причин инцидента, сравнив их действия с практиками СССР.
Кроме того, Китай прокомментировал сообщения о вспышке легочной чумы в Сибири и заявил о сотрудничестве с Россией. Пресс-секретарь китайского МИД Го Цзякунь сообщил, что государства поддерживают тесную связь в вопросах профилактики инфекционных заболеваний и борьбы с ними. Более чем за месяц до инцидента Иркутский противочумный институт завершил совместные с Китаем учения по реагированию на вспышки инфекций.
